updates.name: Henry S. Fitch
updates.bio: University of Kansas herpetologist who lived on the KU Field Station reserve now called the Fitch Reservation from 1948 until not long before he died in 2009. KU calls his herpetological study there, which spanned over 50 years, the longest-running in the world; he also set the reserve's public trail.
updates.research_interests: herpetology; long-term herpetological field study at the KU Field Station
updates.current_affiliation: University of Kansas (Kansas Biological Survey & Center for Ecological Research, KU Field Station)
updates.evidence: public trail set by Henry Fitch, KU herpetologist, who lived with his family here from 1948 until shortly before his death in 2009
updates.notes: Kansas Biological Survey page on the Fitch Natural History Reservation (200). The page does not use the title 'superintendent'; it says the 590-acre reserve was established in 1947 and that Fitch's study spanned more than 50 years. No personal profile page exists (deceased). No ORCID or Scholar link found on a fetched page.

updates.name: Arthur D. Hasler
updates.bio: Zoology faculty member at the University of Wisconsin from 1937, full professor from 1948 and emeritus after retiring in 1978, who expanded the Wisconsin School of Limnology and was central to building the Lake Mendota limnology laboratory and Trout Lake Station. He showed that salmon find natal streams by olfactory imprinting and pioneered whole-lake experiments. He died in 2001.
updates.research_interests: salmon homing and olfactory imprinting; whole-lake experimental manipulations; land-water interactions and lake water quality; cultural eutrophication
updates.current_affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison, Center for Limnology
updates.evidence: Hasler played the key role in the construction of the Laboratory of Limnology on Lake Mendota, and the Trout Lake Station on Trout Lake.
updates.notes: UW-Madison Center for Limnology page 'Arthur Davis Hasler' (200). The page credits him with the key role in building Trout Lake Station but does not call him its director; the lake's role 'former-director' at Trout Lake Station is not confirmed by this page (a research batch should review it). Page also states he was a founder and first director of the Institute for Ecology, NAS member (1969), and died March 23, 2001 aged 93. No ORCID (pre-ORCID era).

updates.name: Amber Packard
updates.bio: Laboratory manager of the Environmental Analysis Lab at the University of the Virgin Islands' Center for Marine and Environmental Studies. The lab supports environmental projects with land- and boat-based sampling, in-situ water testing and analyses of bacteria, suspended solids and nutrients.

updates.name: George R. Aiken
updates.bio: USGS scientist who joined the National Research Program's Central Region in Denver in 1976. The research addressed how natural organic matter, especially dissolved organic carbon, governs groundwater and surface-water biogeochemistry, including permafrost thaw and DOC transport in the Yukon Basin and mercury availability in the Florida Everglades. Continued as a USGS Scientist Emeritus after retiring in 2016.
updates.research_interests: dissolved organic carbon and natural organic matter in groundwater and surface water; permafrost thaw and organic carbon in the Yukon River Basin; organic matter and mercury availability in the Florida Everglades
updates.current_title: Scientist Emeritus, USGS National Research Program (as of 2016)
updates.current_affiliation: U.S. Geological Survey, National Research Program
updates.evidence: George will continue this next phase as a Scientist Emeritus for the USGS National Research Program
updates.notes: Source is the University of Colorado CWEST news item 'Distinguished USGS Scientists, George Aiken, is Retiring' (Dec. 8, 2016); colorado.edu redirects it to the CU Archive-It copy, read with WebFetch (200). USGS staff profile george-aiken returned 403 (george-r-aiken 404). Status left null: the page gives Scientist Emeritus as of 2016 and no fetched page states a later status. updates.name: Ray Bryant
updates.bio: Research soil scientist with USDA-ARS at University Park, Pennsylvania, and a former research leader there, per a 2011 American Society of Agronomy Fellows release. His program studies how soil and landscape processes drive nutrient losses. He earned B.S. and M.S. degrees at Texas Tech and a Ph.D. at Purdue.
updates.research_interests: soil and landscape processes controlling nutrient losses from agricultural land
updates.current_title: Site Coordinator, Upper Chesapeake Bay LTAR; Research Soil Scientist (2011)
updates.current_affiliation: USDA Agricultural Research Service, University Park, Pennsylvania
updates.evidence: Lead investigators: Ray Bryant (site coordinator), Kathy Soder (Grazinglands Lead)
